div.head: 1: INIXODUCT'ION
div.p: In the technological context of today, we have the growing development of distributed time-critical applications, in particular in the Production / Automation systems area. These applications have timing constraints which, if not satisfied, can induce catastrophic situations. Then, implementing such kind of applications requires the use of distributed real-time and faulttolerant computer systems, i.e., responsive sysrems.

Responsive systems have several requirements [Kop,931,among which the schedulability is of the first importance. Two scheduling strategies can be distinguished: static (or pre-run-time) and dynamic scheduling. The scheduling strategy must guarantee the timeliness property. This property, conceming the pre-runtime scheduling strategy, can be evaluated through the evaluation of the worst-cue response time.
Responsive systems in a distributed context are based on communication networks which have then to provide responsive communication services.

In the Production/Automation systems context, an important distributed time-critical application is the physical process control, which is usually based on a Fieldbus [Dec. 931 (low level industrial local network which connects sensors, actuators and automatic controllers).

The goal of this paper is precisely, to present a study which concerns the pre-run-time schedulability analysis in well known Fieldbus networks (Profibus [Pro, 911, FIP [Fip. 911). This paper includes four sections. A first section is concerned by a general presentation of a distributed responsive system by focusing its main constraints (coming from a time-critical application). A second section present the main mechanisms of the Fieldbuses: Profibus and FIP. A third section is concerned by the main formulas establishment for the analysis of the pre-run-time schedulability of both Fieldbuses. A final section describes a comparative example.

div.head: 2: DISTRIBUTEDRESPONSIVE SYSTEMS
div.p: Consider a physical process controlled by a real-time computer system based on a Fieldbus network. The global architecture is presented on the figure 1. We briefly explain it:

The controlled system (real-world) consists of physical elements (sensors and actuators); producer). The real-time attribute of the controlling system results from the interactions with the controlled system (which imposes the timing). The RTEs context is time dependent which induces, in particular, the following problems: temporal validity of a produced information; consistency of the information coming from one producer and consumed by several consumers;

The communication system high-level (called application layer) provides the service of transferring the time dependent information produced by a producer (this information is called a Real-Time Object: RT-0) to the different consumers (the copies in the consumer nodes are called RT-0 images: RT-0,).

In order to solve the consistency problem, we need updating protocols which must have both the atomicity and timeliness properties. Depending on the triggering mechanisms for the start of the RT-0, updating, two approaches can be distinguished [Kop,911: the Event-Triggered (ET) approach where the RT-0; are updated whenever a state meaningful change in an RT-0 occurs; the Time-Triggered (TI') approach,

where the RT-0, updating are periodically initiated at predetermined points in time. The second approach leads to an updating traffic load which is higher than in the Fist one, but which is also completely predictable (the first one induces problems when simultaneous multiple updating are required).

The communication system lower level. and more precisely the link layer has to manage the sharing of the transmission medium for the frame exchanges. The frame exchanges schedulability is an hard point. which must satisfy time constraints (resulting from the time constraints in the higher layers). This approach can also be ET or 'IT. However we have also other causes of information exchanges between the nodes: alarm occurrences; configuration definition messages (which do not necessarily have time constraints). ... .

Then, by considering the distributed responsive system at its link layer service interface, we can summarise the different types of traffic in the following way: we have traffic with timing constraints. i.e., real-time traffic (the real-time traffic can still be subdivided into periodic and sporadic traffics), and traffic without traffic constraints (we call it background traffic). A complete presentation of Profibus and Fip data link layers is out of the scope of this paper. However, some relevant characteristics which enables the support of a responsive system will be summarised in this section.

div.head: I -The Profibus standard [Pro, 911
div.p: A Profibus network has a token passing medium access control method, where the communication can be initiated only by the master station which has the token. The token passing mechanism is an usual solution to solve the medium access conflict in ET systems, since it guarantees that each node orderly receives the rights for transmission on the bus.

The idea behind a timed token protocol is to control the token rotation time. At the network set-up, a protocol parameter called Target Rotation Time (TTR) must be evaluated in order to keep within the system reaction time required by the controlled system. This TTR parameter is user evaluated and must be:
High enough to provide the sufficient time window for all the previously requested messages transfers; Small enough to match the controlled system dynamics;

In systems based on the timed token protocol, the timeliness test is usually based on simulated pattem loads. The remaining question is how valid and truthful are such loads even in burst circumstances. For instance, the Profibus standard suggests an average load based value for the TTR set-up. This is clearly an unacceptable approach for a timeliness system. In this paper we propose a TTR set-up based on the knowledge of the worst-case traffic conditions, which completely guarantees the system timeliness behaviour.

When the token arrives at a node station, the higher priority messages will be. transferred first. Thus, we assign the higher priority to the real-time message set, i.e., to the periodic and sporadic messages.

div.head: . 2 -The FIP standard [Fip, 911
div.p: The FIP network is based on a centralised TDMA control solution, where a central entity, the Bus Arbiter (B.A.), controls all the bus accesses enabling data transfer exchanges between communicating entities. The B.A. manages all messages exchanges according to a pre-defined time-line: the scanning table. This table is organised as a sequence of micro-cycles, the Macro-cycle, which is indefinitely repeated.

During this phase, distant node stations. if addressed, may signalise to the B.A. message pending aperiodic requests (implicit pooling). div.head: -Analysis conclusion
div.p: The Profibus standard, as a classical token bus network, imposes some severe restrictions to the real-time traffic scheduling problem, such as:

Imposing an equal lower bound (H) for all the periods TP; of the periodic streams and all the minimum inter-arrival times of the sporadic streams may lead to a poor network utilisation factor, unless the values of TP; and TS; are all close enough to the H bounding value. In other words, a wide range of values for the parameters TPi and TSj of the real-time traffic , leads to a poor network utilisation factor.
As the background traffic influences the system real-time behaviour (H evaluation), we must bound it (nk messages per node) in order to guarantee the system real-time behaviour.

The Fip standard, based on an TDMA approach, treats the realtime traffic scheduling problem in a more appropriate way. Imposing pre-defined windows (micro-cycles) and a periodic traffic time-line leads to an interesting solution for the periodic traffic scheduling problem. However, some associated drawbacks must be stated:

The interdependency between the length of the dead inferval and the periodic traffic is one of the major drawbacks of the FIP Fieldbus: the timeliness guarantee of the sporadic traffic is not dependent on its intrinsic characteristics, but on the characteristics of other traffics. Also. at the B.A. level, serving the sporadic messages requests in a FIFO basis, leads to an uncontrolled message priority inversion on the bus, and thus it is difficult to guarantee the timeliness of the sporadic paffic.
It's our opinion that:

FIP is an interesting solution to support exchanges between application processes, when the generated real-time traffic is essentially periodic; Profibus, as it not distinguishes between periodic and sporadic traffic, is an interesting solution for essentially sporadic loads.

Our main conclusion is that each one of this standards has its own application field, which is mainly defined by the chosen triggering strategy for exchanging messages between application processes (e.g., the RT-0; updating). The FIP standard is specially suited for TT exchanges, while the Profibus standard is a better solution for ET exchanges.

div.p: Profibus is an interesting solution for essentially sporadic FIP is an interesting solution when the generated real-time 6: CONCLUSION A methodology for analysing the timeliness property (based on the worst-case response time) of Fieldbusses has been presented and a comparison of the Fieldbusses Profibus and FIP has been made. Key elements are the traffic model (the link layer service and the link layer protocol) which is a general concept and the considerations for Profibus and FIP of respectively, the maximum time interval between two consecutive token arrivals in a node, and the dead interval in a node.
The comparison between FIP and Profibus shows that FTP is well suited for supporting periodic real-time traffic, whereas Profibus is an interesting solution for essentially sporadic traffic.
